extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and informed mathematics-interested public (those following formal/computer-assisted proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards and practical desiderata for producing and certifying computer-assisted/formalized mathematical proofs (as exemplified by Hales' Flyspeck project for the Kepler conjecture). Focuses on numerical certifiability, formalization fidelity, tooling, documentation, and sociological acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifiability of computer calculations / numerics
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees could not verify correctness of all of the computer calculations in Hales' 1998/2003 work because those calculations used non-certifiable numerics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerics and computational methods that can be certified or independently verified; avoid black-box numerical computations that cannot be audited. Where numerical results are critical, provide approaches (interval arithmetic, verified numerics, proof-producing computations) that allow formal checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete formalization to an appropriate level
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal verification approach assumes a correct level of formalization — the formal statements and proofs must faithfully capture the intended mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the formalization represents the original mathematical concepts and hypotheses at the correct level of abstraction/detail. Be explicit about modeling choices and assumptions so the formal proof corresponds to the informal argument being certified; avoid under- or over-formalization that changes meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful reproduction of program output
rubrics_metrics.description: One must assume not only correct formalization but also that 'the output faithfully reproduces what the program actually did.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reproducible build/runtime environments, logs, and verifiable traces showing that the formal proof assistant's output corresponds to the intended computations. Cross-check outputs, and where possible, have independent re-checks or re-certifications of program runs to guard against implementation/transcription errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of established automated proof assistants (Isabelle, HOL Light)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flyspeck employed a combination of Isabelle and HOL Light formal proof assistants to certify the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select mature, widely used, and well-understood proof assistants for large formalization projects. Consider tool interoperability, libraries, and community support when choosing systems; document which assistant(s) were used for which parts of the formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to finite configurations and rigorous bounding methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Hales’ original approach reduced the global packing problem to minimizing a function with ~150 variables and obtaining lower bounds for roughly 5000 configurations using linear programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When facing a complex global problem, reduce it to a finite (but checkable) set of cases and provide rigorous bounds for each case using methods (e.g., linear programming) that can be audited and, where applicable, formalized. Make the decomposition and bounding strategy explicit so it can be independently examined and formalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive documentation and availability of code/data/results
rubrics_metrics.description: Hales and Ferguson documented their project with 250 pages of notes and three Gbyte of computer code, data and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish full documentation, source code, data, and computational artifacts necessary to reproduce and audit the computational parts of the proof. Organize materials clearly and provide instructions for independent verification; archive artifacts in durable, accessible repositories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit statement of residual uncertainty / referee limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Annals refereeing panel reported being '99% certain' the proof was sound, but they could not verify all computer calculations, and the journal initially considered a caveat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing computer-assisted proofs, explicitly state any remaining points of uncertainty or limitations of human referees' ability to check computations. Explain which parts have been formally certified, which rely on unverified computations, and what steps are planned/possible to close gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociological acceptance and community impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments suggest Hales’ use of automated proof assistants is a significant sociological milestone and could become a norm; one quote: 'A world-famous mathematician has turned his hand toward automated theorem proving; that kind of sociological fact is very important.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and report on the broader community acceptance and implications of formalized proofs: how the approach affects peer review, standards of correctness, tooling adoption, and training. Consider outreach and documentation to help the community understand and trust automated certification methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim of formal proof completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Flyspeck project announced completion of a computer-verified formal proof of the Kepler conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a completed formal proof, provide a clear statement of coverage (which lemmas/theorems/cases are fully formalized), the repository/artefacts proving completion, and verification that no informal gaps remain. Include a checklist or map from informal proof components to their formal counterparts.
